newsitem.title: USA: September wholesale sales drop sharply.
newsitem.headline: September wholesale sales drop sharply.

text.p: Inventories of goods on wholesalers' shelves dropped at the sharpest rate in 14-1/2 years during September, the Commerce Department said on Friday, as sales picked up from an August slump.
Overall inventories fell 1.3 percent to a seasonally adjusted $255.52 billion -- the biggest monthly decline since a 1.6 percent plunge in February 1982, the department said.
The unexpected plunge in stocks of unsold goods prompted uneasiness in financial markets as analysts speculated the way was being cleared for a quickened pace of industrial output.
Both stock and bond prices were moderately lower in afternoon trading.

"It seems that we apparently had significantly less inventory accumulation in the third quarter than originally estimated by the Commerce Department," said Robert Dederick, economic consultant to Northern Trust Co. in Chicago.
"So it suggests that any concerns that inventories would act as a drag on growth in the fourth quarter are somewhat eased by the new data," Dederick added.
The figures cover only wholesalers' activities, however, and a full report on retailers' and manufacturers' combined September inventories will not be available for another week.
The sharp drop in wholesaler inventories was contrary to Wall Street economists' forecast of a 0.3 percent September increase.
In addition, August inventories were revised to show a 0.1 percent decrease -- instead of the 0.5 percent rise in unsold stocks that the government had reported a month ago.
The Commerce Department previously reported that third-quarter economic growth slowed sharply to a 2.2 percent annual rate from 4.7 percent in the second quarter.

That was viewed positively by financial markets as an indication that inflationary pressures were likely to remain muted. The Federal Reserve's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets next Wednesday to plot interest-rate strategy and most analysts speculate it will not need to raise rates.
Total wholesale sales increased 0.9 percent in September to $201.97 billion after falling a revised 1 percent in August. Previously, the department said August sales had declined 0.9 percent.
As a result, the inventory-to-sales ratio, which measures how long it would take to deplete inventories at the current sales pace, fell to 1.27 months' worth from 1.29 months in August.
That was the lowest level for the inventory-to-sales ratio in more than six years, since it was also at 1.27 months in August 1990.
Stocks of both durable and nondurable goods were drawn down in September.
There was a big 4 percent drop in motor vehicle and equipment inventories from August levels and smaller declines in electrical goods and metals.
Similarly, inventories of nondurables like farm-product raw materials, groceries and clothing fell sharply from August levels.
